Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence (basis for Year Established): Agrippa I's letter to Gaius (Caligula), quoted by Philo, Legatio ad Gaium 281 (c. 40 CE, the statue crisis), lists Jewish colonies in Greece including 'Corinth and all the most fertile and wealthiest districts of Peloponnesus'. Implies a settled community; no count. Context (from other sources): Corinth was destroyed by Mummius in 146 BCE and refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BCE; no evidence of Jews in Hellenistic Corinth before 146 BCE was found.

Acts 18:1-8: Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla, Jews recently come from Italy after Claudius ordered the Jews out of Rome (c. 49 CE); Paul reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath; Crispus, the leader of the synagogue (archisynagogos), believes with his household; Titius Justus' house is next to the synagogue. Organized community with a synagogue building and officers; no count. c. 50 CE (Paul's 18-month stay c. 50-51, dated by Gallio's proconsulship).

Acts 18:12-17: the Jews of Corinth bring Paul before Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, who refuses to judge; the crowd beats Sosthenes, the official of the synagogue. Gallio's proconsulship is dated c. 51-52 CE (Delphi inscription); c. 51 CE. Community large enough to act collectively before the governor; no count.

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Corinth': Jews lived in Corinth as in other cities of Greece (Philo, Legatio §36); Paul preached 18 months in the synagogue and baptized the archisynagogue Crispus; the scandal before the governor Gallio shows 'a large number of Jews at Corinth'; Sosthenes probably Crispus' successor. Qualitative assessment only, no figure. c. 51 CE (Gallio).

Encyclopaedia Judaica (via Jewish Virtual Library), 'Corinth': Paul spent one and a half years in Corinth preaching in the synagogue on Sabbaths; Aquila and Priscilla (weavers) came from Rome when Claudius expelled the Jews; Corinthian Jewry apparently belonged to the lower classes. c. 50 CE (Paul's stay). No count.

Livius.org, 'Roman Corinth': population of the Roman colony was mixed Greeks and Roman veterans, with 'a substantial Jewish minority'. Undated statement about Roman Corinth; 1st c. CE midpoint (50) used. Qualitative, no count.

Acts 18:27-19:1: Apollos, an Alexandrian Jew, crosses to Achaia and 'powerfully refuted the Jews in public'; Acts 19:1 places him in Corinth. Implies a continuing Jewish community after Paul's departure. c. 52 CE.

1 Corinthians 1:14 and 7:18 (letter commonly dated c. 53-55 CE; c. 54 used): Paul baptized Crispus (the former synagogue leader of Acts 18:8) in Corinth, and addresses members of the Corinthian church who were circumcised when called, i.e. Jewish-born residents. No count.

Josephus, War 3.10.10 (3.532-542): after the capture of Taricheae (8 Gorpieus, autumn 67 CE) Vespasian chose 'six thousand of the strongest' Jewish young men and sent them to Nero 'to dig through the Isthmus' (Nero's Corinth canal); 1,200 old/useless killed and 30,400 sold as slaves. These were Galilean war captives used as forced labour at the Isthmus, not resident Jews of Corinth, so the 6000 is NOT entered as Population.
